checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Pick one scene: a finished level of your own, or the level of the template. Save a camera bookmark, which is a stored camera position, so that every capture uses the same view.
Open Settings > Engine Scalability Settings. Capture the view on Low and on Epic, with stat unit visible in both captures.

Create the file Config/DefaultScalability.ini in the project. In it, override one quality group, for example the sections [FoliageQuality@0] to [FoliageQuality@2]. Restart the editor and check that the change works.
If you use foliage, turn on Enable Density Scaling on the foliage types. Then compare the console commands sg.FoliageQuality 0 and sg.FoliageQuality 3.

Open a material that is used in the scene, or make one with an extra detail branch, such as a second texture that is multiplied in. Add a Quality Switch node that removes the costly branch on Low. Check the result with the Shader Complexity view mode.
Type the name of one sg.* setting in the console with no value after it. Note the current value that it prints and where that value was set.

TAQ26.brief: Interchange is the system Unreal uses to import files such as meshes and textures. Each import goes through a pipeline stack, which is an ordered list of pipelines, and each pipeline can change how the asset is created. If you add your own pipeline, your team's rules are applied to every import, and nobody has to fix each asset by hand. In this quest you write a Blueprint pipeline that enforces one rule and add it to the import stack of a project.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open Project Settings and go to Engine, then Interchange. Take a screenshot of the pipeline stack that is used for Import Content.
Create a Blueprint class with the parent class InterchangePipelineBase. Name it BP_IP_StudioRules.
Override the function Scripted Execute Pipeline or the function Scripted Execute Post Import Pipeline. Make it enforce one rule, for example a name prefix such as SM_, or a fixed LOD Group.
Add BP_IP_StudioRules to the pipeline stack of the project. Put it after the default pipelines.

Import 3 test meshes. If you have no mesh files, export three from Unreal first: right-click a Static Mesh, such as a cube, choose Asset Actions, then Export, and save it as an FBX file under three different names. Use Preview in the import window to check the assets before you click Import.
Change one of the source files and reimport it. Check that the same stack and options come back.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Build a test level with Nanite rock and building meshes, one mesh that is not Nanite, and a foliage mesh with a WPO wind material. Simple stand-ins work: boxes and dense spheres made in Modeling Mode with Nanite enabled, one cube without Nanite, and a few meshes with a material in which a Sine of a Time node, multiplied by a small vector, is connected to World Position Offset. Use one Directional Light.
Keep the camera still. Switch the viewport to View Modes > Virtual Shadow Map > Cached Page. Take a screenshot of the red areas, which are the pages that are not cached.
Use the Shadow Casters view to find what invalidates the pages. Fix one cause: either set World Position Offset Disable Distance, or change Shadow Cache Invalidation Behavior.
Run the console commands r.ShaderPrintEnable 1 and r.Shadow.Virtual.Stats 1. Note the numbers of Allocated, Cached and Invalidated pages before and after your fix.
Open the Nanite Visualization menu. Check the Overdraw view and the Evaluate WPO view on your foliage.
Capture a short Unreal Insights trace. Find the Shadow Depths cost for VSM before and after your fix.

Use a test project that has Substrate turned on. To make one, create a project from the Third Person template, open Project Settings, go to Rendering, turn on Substrate materials and restart the editor. In Project Settings > Rendering, check which GBuffer format it uses.
Create a material named M_Sub_CarPaint. Use a metal Slab as the base and put a clear coat Slab on top of it with a Substrate Vertical Layer node. Expose Top Thickness as a parameter.
Create a material named M_Sub_WetGround. Mix two Slabs side by side with a Substrate Horizontal Blend node, and drive the mix with a mask texture.
In the Material Editor, open Window > Substrate and read the stats for both materials. Note the bytes per pixel and any simplification that is reported.
Turn on Use Parameter Blending on the last operator node before the root node. Compare the stats and the look with the earlier result.
In the level, put both materials on screen. Check the view modes View Modes > Substrate > Material Count and Material Classification.

TAQ29.brief: The most useful work of a technical artist is often a tool or a library that other people use every day. In this quest you make one finished piece that someone else can install and use. You choose between an import or naming tool and a library of material functions, write the documentation, let another person test it, and check how a scene that uses it holds up on Low and Epic quality. Everything you need to build is listed in the steps.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Pick one path. Path A is an import or naming tool: an Interchange pipeline, an Editor Utility Widget (EUW_), or a validator based on EditorValidatorBase. Path B is a library of at least 6 material functions with names that start with MF_.
Write short documentation. It should say what the piece does, how to install it, its rules or inputs, and one known limit.
For Path A, make the tool report clear errors in the Message Log, and run it on a full folder. For Path B, build 3 materials from the library and document the inputs of each function.

Give it to at least one other person. They use it on their own assets and tell you what worked and what did not. If nobody can test it, migrate it into a new empty project and use it there yourself, following only your documentation.
Fix at least one problem that the test found, and write the change down in a change log.
Do a scalability check. Take one scene that uses your work, capture it on Low and on Epic from the same camera bookmark with stat unit visible, and note the biggest difference.
TAQ29.done_when: Send a writeup that contains the documentation of the tool or library, a short video clip (30 seconds or less) or screenshots of it running, the feedback from the test and your fix, and the Low and Epic screenshots with 2 to 3 lines on the result. A mentor must approve it.

checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open a level that uses many textures. If you have none, place several mannequins and other textured meshes in the level of the template. Run Build > Build Texture Streaming.
Start PIE and run the console command STAT STREAMING. Write down the values of Streaming Pool, Required Pool and Wanted Mips.
Lower the value of r.Streaming.PoolSize until Required Pool goes over 100%. Take a screenshot that shows which surfaces go blurry first.
Check the view modes Mesh UV Density Accuracy and Material Texture Scale Accuracy. Find one object that is shown in red or green.
Fix one cause. For example, change the Streaming Distance Multiplier on a mesh, or fix a texture that is far too big for its size on the screen.
Set the pool back to its old value. Compare the STAT STREAMING numbers from before and after your fix.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open the Content Browser. Click the Filters drop-down and add the Static Mesh filter. Then add the Material filter. Note that you now see both types.
In the search bar, type Triangles>1500 and see which meshes remain. Then try the search Type==Blueprint.
Create a custom filter: open Filters, then Custom Filter, and click Create New Filter. Name it HeavyMeshes, pick a color, and enter Triangles>5000 as the Filter String.
In the Collections panel, click Add (+) and choose Local Collection. Name the collection Col_Hero_Props.
Add at least 3 assets to the collection. You can right-click an asset and choose Manage Collections, or you can drag the assets onto the collection.
Right-click a filter in the Filters area and try Enable Only This. Then use Disable All Filters.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. In the Content Browser, right-click a Material Instance, for example one of the material instances of the mannequin, and choose Reference Viewer.
Read the graph. The assets on the left reference your asset, which means they use it. The assets on the right are referenced by your asset.
Press D once to increase the dependency search depth, so the graph shows one more step to the right. Press R once to increase the referencer search depth on the left.
Press H to hide hard references, and then press H again to show them. Press S to do the same with soft references.
Right-click the node of your asset and use Copy Referencing Objects List. Paste the text into a notepad.
Right-click the node again and choose Make Collection With to create a collection of the assets that reference it.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. In the Content Browser, right-click a Level asset, or a Blueprint that has meshes and materials, such as BP_ThirdPersonCharacter, and choose Size Map.
Read the boxes. A bigger box means a bigger asset. A box inside another box means that the outer asset references the inner one.
Use the mouse wheel to zoom. Double-click the biggest box so that it fills the window.
Switch the size type between disk size and memory size, and note that the numbers are different.
Find the single largest asset in the map. Right-click its box to browse to it or to open it.
Open a Static Mesh in the Static Mesh Editor. Use Asset > Size Map (Alt + Shift + M) to see the size map of that mesh too.
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open the Asset Audit window with Window > Developer Tools > Asset Audit. The window is empty when it opens.
Click Add Chunks to fill the window with a summary of the chunks in the project.
Select a Texture in the Content Browser, right-click it, and open the Reference Viewer. Right-click the node there and choose Audit Assets to add it to the audit.
Add 5 or more textures or meshes to the audit and compare their rows.
Open the Settings menu, which is the gear icon at the top right, and export the list to a .csv file.
Right-click a chunk row and open its Size Map.
Create a second, empty project. This is your target project. Close it after it has been created.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. This is your main project. In it, select a Material Instance and a Blueprint that uses a mesh, for example a material instance of the mannequin and BP_ThirdPersonCharacter. Hold Ctrl while you click to select both.
Right-click one of the selected assets and choose Asset Actions, then Migrate.
Read the Asset Report window. Count how many extra assets it will copy, such as textures, meshes and parent materials.
Click OK. Then select the Content folder of the target project and click Select Folder.
Open the target project and confirm that the material and the Blueprint look correct.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Create a folder named Content/Test_Redirect. In it, make a Material named M_RedirectTest and a Material Instance named MI_RedirectTest that is based on that material.
Move M_RedirectTest to a new folder named Content/Test_Redirect/Moved.
In the Content Browser, open Filter, then Other Filters, and enable Show Redirectors. Find the redirector that was left in the old location.
Switch to Filter, then Miscellaneous, then Redirectors. Note that now only redirectors are shown.
Right-click the redirector and choose Fixup. Check that the redirector disappears and that MI_RedirectTest still works.
Write one sentence about what happened to the packages (the asset files) that pointed to the redirector.
